name: Revision rhinoplasty

lead: Revision rhinoplasty is surgery to fix aesthetic or functional problems after a previous rhinoplasty, such as tip drop, asymmetry, collapse, a pinched tip or breathing difficulty. People use it to get a more balanced nose after a first result they were unhappy with.

A general reference puts the share of primary operations needing revision at 5 to 20 percent. On looksmax.org, members ask whether a drooping tip a year after surgery needs a full redo or a minor closed procedure, and discuss factors such as jaw support. Literature covers conchal cartilage grafts for valve collapse, irradiated costal cartilage, Gore-Tex, porous polyethylene and silicone implants.

paras: Revisions are usually done by an open approach and often use cartilage from the ear or rib, or implants, to rebuild support. The corrected shape shows after healing.

Revision is technically more complex than primary surgery. Reports describe complications from implants and graft materials, persisting obstruction, and dissatisfaction. A study of rhinoplasty candidates found a high prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder symptoms. It is performed by surgeons under anaesthesia.

angle.text: Revision rhinoplasty is for people unhappy with a first nose job who want shape or breathing problems corrected, such as asymmetry, a dropped tip or collapse. Surgeons rebuild support with cartilage grafts or implants, and the corrected shape shows after healing. Revision rates of roughly 5 to 20 percent are documented in surgical references.

lead: Revision rhinoplasty, or secondary rhinoplasty, is a nose operation performed after a previous rhinoplasty to address aesthetic or functional problems. A general reference gives 5 to 20 percent as the share of primary operations needing a second procedure and lists typical problems such as breathing deficits, asymmetry, collapse, a hanging columella, a pinched tip and a scooped nose.[1] A study of a plastic surgery group practice examined cosmetic rhinoplasty revision rates and risk factors for dissatisfaction.[2]

Revision surgery commonly uses open approaches and cartilage grafts or implants, and the literature includes long-term series on Gore-Tex, porous high-density polyethylene, irradiated homologous costal cartilage and silicone implants.[3][4][5][6] A review of risks and complications describes the range of problems after rhinoplasty.[7]
In looksmaxxing communities it appears in individual cases where a member asks about a tip that dropped after surgery.[8]
infobox: Septum, ear (conchal), rib; implants such as Gore-Tex, polyethylene

paras: Cited causes include over-resection leading to collapse or breathing problems, asymmetry and tip problems.[1] Weakness or collapse of upper lateral cartilages after rhinoplasty can cause internal valve dysfunction, treated in one 72-patient series with a conchal cartilage butterfly graft.[9]
A study of 226 rhinoplasty candidates reported a high prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder symptoms among people seeking the operation.[10]

Reported experience includes a 10-year series of Gore-Tex nasal augmentation covering 309 patients, an earlier 6-year experience, use of porous high-density polyethylene in revision and in platyrrhine noses, a long-term follow-up of irradiated homologous costal cartilage, and a gross and pathologic analysis of long-term silicone implants removed in 221 revision cases.[3][11][4][5][6]
A study of long-term patient satisfaction after revision rhinoplasty examined outcomes of secondary surgery.[12] The sources reviewed do not give a single satisfaction figure.

One looksmax.org poster described a tip that dropped back a few months after surgery for a large drooping nose and asked whether fillers or a tip rhinoplasty were needed. Replies suggested consulting the original or another surgeon about a minor closed procedure, and one member speculated that a recessed maxilla failed to support the tip and planned jaw surgery.[8] These are individual opinions, not clinical findings.

Human data are mostly retrospective: revision-rate analysis, implant series (Gore-Tex, polyethylene, silicone, costal cartilage), a series on butterfly grafts for post-rhinoplasty valve dysfunction, a long-term satisfaction study after revision, and a body dysmorphic disorder prevalence study.[2][3][4][5][6][9][10][12] No randomised trial of revision rhinoplasty appears in the sources reviewed.

lore.intro: Revision appears on looksmax.org in individual case threads, where members consider the cause of an undesired result.[8]

claims.claim: A nose tip that relapses after surgery can be caused by insufficient support from a recessed maxilla.
A dropped tip may need only a minor closed procedure rather than a full revision.

timeline.event: Six-year experience with Gore-Tex in rhinoplasty published.[11]
Ten-year Gore-Tex nasal augmentation series published.[3]
